clinicalPearls: Caused by compression of the left renal vein, most often the anterior (classic) type where it is squeezed between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta, or the posterior type where a retroaortic left renal vein is compressed between the aorta and vertebral column
Nutcracker phenomenon describes the anatomical compression on imaging; nutcracker syndrome denotes compression that produces symptoms
Typical features are left-sided haematuria (micro- or macroscopic), left flank or abdominal pain, and orthostatic proteinuria
In men it may cause a left varicocele and in women pelvic congestion symptoms owing to raised gonadal vein pressure
Tends to occur in slender individuals with little retroperitoneal fat, and symptoms may worsen with upright posture or exertion
Diagnosis integrates Doppler ultrasound, cross-sectional venous imaging, and, when needed, venography with pressure gradient measurement
Management ranges from conservative observation (many young patients improve with growth and weight gain) to left renal vein transposition, stenting, or other surgical options for severe disease
reference.pathophysiology: Nutcracker syndrome results from mechanical compression of the left renal vein along its course to the inferior vena cava. In the anterior variant the vein is entrapped in the narrowed angle between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta; in the posterior variant a retroaortic vein is compressed between the aorta and the spine. Compression raises pressure within the left renal vein and its tributaries, causing venous congestion, development of collaterals, and rupture of thin-walled veins into the collecting system, which produces haematuria. Raised pressure transmitted to the gonadal vein underlies varicocele in men and pelvic congestion in women.
additionalDifferentials: Glomerular causes of haematuria (e.g. IgA nephropathy, thin basement membrane disease)
Urolithiasis causing loin pain and haematuria
Pelvic congestion syndrome from other cause
additionalInvestigations: Doppler ultrasound of the left renal vein to assess flow velocities and compression
CT or MR venography to demonstrate the compressed segment and anatomy
Retrograde venography with renocaval pressure gradient measurement in equivocal cases
Urinalysis to confirm haematuria and quantify proteinuria (including orthostatic testing)
Cystoscopy to lateralise bleeding to the left ureteric orifice when macroscopic haematuria is present
Exclusion of glomerular disease with appropriate renal workup
redFlags: Severe or recurrent macroscopic haematuria causing anaemia or clot retention
Progressive proteinuria or evidence of renal impairment
Debilitating flank or pelvic pain unresponsive to conservative measures
Features suggesting an alternative serious cause such as malignancy
reference.prognosis: Many younger patients improve spontaneously as retroperitoneal fat increases with growth, and conservative management is often sufficient; those with severe, persistent symptoms generally respond well to renal vein transposition or endovascular stenting, though stent-related complications can occur.
pitfalls: Diagnosing the syndrome from imaging compression alone without correlating symptoms (over-diagnosis of an incidental phenomenon)
Missing a coexisting glomerular cause of haematuria
Placing an endovascular stent prematurely in a young patient likely to improve conservatively
Overlooking the posterior (retroaortic) variant on imaging
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
management: Conservative observation in younger, mildly symptomatic patients, as many improve spontaneously with growth and increasing retroperitoneal fat
Weight-gain measures where low body mass contributes, with analgesia for flank pain
Renal vein transposition or other open surgical repair for severe, persistent haematuria or pain refractory to conservative care
Endovascular stenting of the left renal vein as an alternative, with vigilance for stent migration and thrombosis
Monitoring of haematuria, proteinuria and anaemia, with treatment of an associated left varicocele or pelvic congestion
Referral to urology or vascular surgery for intervention decisions after confirmatory venographic pressure-gradient measurement
